a: Hypothesis testing evaluates evidence against a null hypothesis using a test statistic and p-value.
A p-value is the probability of data as extreme as observed if the null is true.
A confidence interval ranges plausible values for a parameter at a confidence level.
Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis (false positive).
Type II error fails to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative).
Common assumptions: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, residual normality.
Bayesian updates beliefs with priors; frequentist focuses on long-run procedure properties.
Sampling methods include simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling.
A/B tests estimate treatment effects and uncertainty; watch multiple testing and peeking.
Extreme observations tend to be followed by more average ones purely statistically.
